claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar architecture.
The baseline lamellar colonies contain numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar boundaries serve as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Adding less than 1 at% Zr will improve both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility.
A less-than-1-at% Zr addition will promote Zr segregation to internal lamellar interfaces.
Zr segregation at lamellar interfaces will enhance interfacial cohesion.
More cohesive interfaces will reduce local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation.
Zr-strengthened interfaces will impede microcrack propagation.
Zr-strengthened lamellar interfaces will act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Interfacial strengthening will produce simultaneous gains in tensile strength and ductility.
The unmodified baseline suffers early microcrack initiation because of weak interfacial bonding.
The Zr-modified alloy will show statistically significant increases in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline.
The Zr-modified alloy will form fewer microcracks during room-temperature tensile loading.
The beneficial effect requires the Zr concentration to remain below 1 at%.
The beneficial effect requires processing conditions that promote effective interfacial segregation.
Excessive Zr or unsuitable heat treatment may form secondary phases or disrupt the eutectic lamellar structure, eliminating the benefit.
The quantitative mechanical-property enhancement may depend on processing variations and the specific alloy chemistry.

contradictions.description: The experiment describes both sets as having the same composition, although one set contains an added Zr concentration and the other contains no Zr. This is consistent only if 'same composition' is interpreted as the same parent composition before Zr addition.
